concept.name: Dead Letter Queues

relationships.description: Connects Dead Letter Queues to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: A secondary quarantine queue that captures messages a consumer repeatedly fails to process after a bounded number of retries, preventing poison pills from blocking healthy traffic.
spark.keyTakeaway: A DLQ is not a trash can—it requires preserved failure metadata, bounded retention, alerting, and an idempotent replay mechanism.

concept.whyItMatters: Without a Dead Letter Queue, a single malformed payload ('poison pill') or unexpected null field causes a consumer to crash, nack, and re-queue the same message in an infinite loop—consuming 100% of worker CPU, saturating downstream DB connections, and stalling millions of valid messages behind it. A DLQ isolates the bad message after N attempts so the main pipeline keeps flowing while engineers inspect and replay the failure.
whenToUse: Asynchronous event-driven pipelines (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) where malformed schemas, unexpected business states, or transient downstream outages can fail individual messages.
High-value workflows (payments, order fulfillment, webhooks) where silently dropping failed messages is unacceptable.
Batch or streaming consumers where one poison-pill record must not halt partition progress for healthy records.
whenNotToUse: Fire-and-forget telemetry (e.g., non-critical clickstream metrics or debug logs) where dropping a malformed event is cheaper than operating replay tooling.
Strict FIFO ordered streams where skipping a failed message for key `K` and processing message `K+1` would corrupt state (requires per-key blocking or stateful retry queues instead).
Synchronous request/response APIs where the caller is waiting on an immediate HTTP 4xx/5xx error.
keyPoints: Trigger DLQ routing via a bounded retry threshold—such as AWS SQS `maxReceiveCount = 5` on a redrive policy, or RabbitMQ `x-dead-letter-exchange` on `basic.nack(requeue=false)`.

In Kafka, consumers do not block a partition forever; best practice uses tiered retry topics (`topic.retry.1m`, `topic.retry.10m`) before routing to `topic.dlq` with original key, offset, and stack-trace headers.

Distinguish permanent errors (400 Bad Request, schema deserialization failure—route to DLQ immediately) from transient errors (503 Service Unavailable, DB deadlock—retry with exponential backoff + jitter).
Every DLQ message must carry diagnostic headers: `x-exception-class`, `x-exception-message`, `x-original-topic`, `x-retry-count`, and `x-failed-at`.
Replaying a DLQ requires idempotent consumers; otherwise re-driving a message that partially succeeded before failing will duplicate side effects like double-charging a customer.

examples.title: Isolating poison-pill webhooks in AWS SQS
examples.scenario: A SaaS billing worker processes Stripe webhooks from an SQS queue. A rare legacy event lacks a `customer_id` field, causing a `NullPointerException` on every attempt and starving 20,000 valid webhooks.
examples.outcome: Configuring an SQS Redrive Policy with `maxReceiveCount = 3` and exponential visibility-timeout backoff moves the malformed webhook to `billing-webhooks-dlq` within 90 seconds, keeping main queue p99 lag under 500ms while alerting on-call.

examples.title: Non-blocking Kafka retry topics in an order pipeline
examples.scenario: An inventory consumer reads `orders.created` across 12 partitions. When a downstream warehouse API times out for 5 minutes, blocking the partition halts all orders.
examples.outcome: Using Spring Kafka `@RetryableTopic(attempts = '4', backoff = @Backoff(delay = 10000, multiplier = 3))`, transient failures move to `orders.created-retry-0..2` and ultimately `orders.created-dlt`, preserving main partition throughput.

tradeOffs.factor: Immediate DLQ vs. Delayed Retry Topics
tradeOffs.pro: Retry topics with 1m/10m/1h delays automatically heal transient outages without waking on-call.
tradeOffs.con: Adds topic proliferation and breaks strict global message ordering.

tradeOffs.pro: Routing bad messages to a DLQ keeps throughput high for all other keys in the partition.
tradeOffs.con: Out-of-order execution can occur if a later event for the same entity succeeds while the earlier event sits in the DLQ.

tradeOffs.factor: Long DLQ Retention vs. Storage Cost
tradeOffs.pro: Retaining DLQ messages for 14–30 days gives teams time to deploy a bugfix and replay safely.
tradeOffs.con: Unmonitored DLQs can silently accumulate millions of stale events that are no longer safe to replay.

failureModes.name: DLQ Graveyard (write-only queue)
failureModes.description: Messages land in the DLQ with no CloudWatch/Prometheus alerts, no retention policy, and no replay runbook—silently losing customer data.
failureModes.mitigation: Alert when `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible > 0` (or DLQ rate > threshold) and review/drain DLQs weekly.

failureModes.name: Infinite DLQ-to-Main redrive loop
failureModes.description: An operator blindly replays 5,000 DLQ messages back to the main queue without fixing the underlying bug or schema mismatch, re-triggering an outage.
failureModes.mitigation: Inspect sample payloads and `x-exception-message` headers first, deploy and verify the fix, then redrive at a rate-limited pace (e.g., 50 msg/sec).

failureModes.name: Serialization crash before retry tracking
failureModes.description: A corrupted JSON/Avro payload throws an exception in the Kafka deserializer before the consumer's retry wrapper runs, crashing the consumer pod in an infinite CrashLoopBackOff.
failureModes.mitigation: Wrap deserializers in `ErrorHandlingDeserializer` so malformed bytes are captured and routed straight to the DLQ.

failureModes.name: Out-of-order state corruption on replay
failureModes.description: An `OrderCreated` event fails and goes to the DLQ; `OrderCancelled` arrives later, is ignored, and then `OrderCreated` is replayed—resurrecting a cancelled order.
failureModes.mitigation: Include entity `version` or `event_timestamp` checks in consumers so stale replayed events do not overwrite newer state.

commonMistakes: Retrying permanent 4xx/validation errors 10 times with backoff instead of routing them to the DLQ on attempt 1.
Using the same visibility timeout for every retry instead of exponential backoff, causing a thundering herd against a recovering downstream database.
Dropping original Kafka keys, correlation IDs, or exception stack traces when forwarding a message to the DLQ.
Forgetting to set a `MessageRetentionPeriod` (e.g., 14 days in SQS) or disk quota on the DLQ, risking premature message expiration.
Replaying DLQ messages into non-idempotent consumers, causing duplicate emails, duplicate charges, or corrupted inventory counts.

sections.content:
## The idea

In asynchronous messaging systems, a **Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)** is a dedicated quarantine destination for messages that cannot be processed successfully after a configured number of attempts. Instead of letting a single unprocessable message ('poison pill') crash a worker repeatedly or block a queue partition indefinitely, the broker or consumer framework moves the message aside.

Crucially, a DLQ is an **operational safety valve, not a permanent solution**. Its job is to preserve the main pipeline's availability while retaining enough payload and error context for an engineer (or automated redrive job) to diagnose the root cause, fix the bug or data, and replay the message safely.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an order-fulfillment consumer reading from an `orders.events` queue with a 3-tier retry policy:

1. **Transient failure**: Worker pulls `Order #8821`, calls the Shipping API, and gets `503 Service Unavailable`. Because `503` is retryable, it nacks with a 30s delay (`retryCount = 1`).
2. **Escalating backoff**: Subsequent attempts at +2m and +10m still fail (or a `NullPointerException` occurs due to a missing postal code—a non-retryable bug).
3. **Dead-letter routing**: Once `receiveCount == maxReceiveCount (3)` (or immediately for `DeserializationException`), the broker/consumer attaches metadata headers (`x-exception-message`, `x-original-topic`, `x-failed-at`) and routes `Order #8821` to `orders.events.dlq`.
4. **Alert & replay**: Prometheus fires an alert on `dlq_messages_total > 0`. An engineer inspects the payload, deploys a null-safe fix, and runs a rate-limited redrive script to replay `Order #8821` back into `orders.events`.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Broker mechanics: SQS vs. RabbitMQ vs. Kafka
sections.content:
## Broker mechanics: SQS vs. RabbitMQ vs. Kafka

**AWS SQS** handles DLQs natively via a `RedrivePolicy` (`deadLetterTargetArn` and `maxReceiveCount`). When a consumer fails to delete a message before `VisibilityTimeout` expires `N` times, SQS moves it atomically to the DLQ—and even provides a built-in StartMessageMoveTask API for rate-limited redrive.

**RabbitMQ** uses a Dead Letter Exchange (`x-dead-letter-exchange`). Messages move there when rejected via `basic.nack(requeue=false)`, when per-message TTL expires, or when queue length exceeds `x-max-length`.

**Apache Kafka** has no broker-level DLQ because partitions are immutable append-only logs. Instead, the consumer framework (Spring Kafka, Kafka Connect `errors.tolerance=all`) catches failures, commits the main offset so the partition advances, and produces the failed record + headers to a `.dlq` topic.

## Error classification & routing policy

| Error Category | Examples | Retry Policy | DLQ Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Poison Pill / Schema** | `JsonParseException`, Avro mismatch | 0 retries (permanent) | Route to DLQ immediately with raw bytes |
| **Validation / Business** | Invalid `currency`, missing `orderId` | 0 retries (permanent) | Route to DLQ + alert producer team |
| **Downstream Outage** | HTTP `503`, `SocketTimeoutException` | 3–5 retries, exponential backoff | Route to DLQ only after budget exhausted |
| **DB Lock / Deadlock** | PostgreSQL `40P01`, OptimisticLock | 3 fast retries (100ms–1s + jitter) | Route to DLQ if contention persists |

## Failure modes

The most dangerous failure mode is **out-of-order state resurrection during replay**. If `OrderCreated` sits in a DLQ for 2 hours while `OrderCancelled` is processed on the main queue, replaying `OrderCreated` naively can overwrite the `CANCELLED` state. Every consumer must check monotonic entity versions or timestamps before applying state.

Another common failure is **unbounded redrive thundering herds**: dumping 100,000 DLQ messages back into the main queue at full speed overwhelms the downstream database again. Always throttle redrives (e.g., 50–200 msg/sec) and monitor downstream CPU/connection pools.

## Observability & safe replay architecture

Treat DLQ depth as a first-class SLO indicator. Emit metrics tagged by `topic`, `error_class`, and `consumer_group`, and sample DLQ payloads into an indexed log store (scrubbing PII) so engineers don't have to SSH into brokers to read raw bytes.

For replay, support filtering by time window or error class so you can redrive `503` timeouts from an outage window without accidentally replaying known invalid payloads.

## Practical checklist

- Separate permanent errors (0 retries) from transient errors (exponential backoff + jitter).
- Attach `x-original-topic`, `x-exception-message`, `x-retry-count`, and `x-failed-at` headers to every DLQ record.
- Wrap Kafka deserializers with `ErrorHandlingDeserializer` so corrupt bytes don't crash-loop consumers.
- Enforce idempotency keys and entity version checks on consumers before enabling DLQ replay.
- Set an alert on `dlq_depth > 0` and configure rate-limited redrive tooling.

interviewProblems.title: Dead Letter Queues
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Dead Letter Queues. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A secondary quarantine queue that captures messages a consumer repeatedly fails to process after a bounded number of retries, preventing poison pills from blocking healthy traffic.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Retry / Backoff applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Dead Letter Queue.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Dead Letter Queue experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Alert when `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible > 0` (or DLQ rate > threshold) and review/drain DLQs weekly.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: A DLQ is not a trash can—it requires preserved failure metadata, bounded retention, alerting, and an idempotent replay mechanism.
Avoid trap: Retrying permanent 4xx/validation errors 10 times with backoff instead of routing them to the DLQ on attempt 1.
Avoid trap: Using the same visibility timeout for every retry instead of exponential backoff, causing a thundering herd against a recovering downstream database.
When to reach for it: Asynchronous event-driven pipelines (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) where malformed schemas, unexpected business states, or transient downstream outages can fail individual messages.
When to reach for it: High-value workflows (payments, order fulfillment, webhooks) where silently dropping failed messages is unacceptable.

putItTogether.title: Putting Dead Letter Queues Together
putItTogether.summary: A DLQ is not a trash can—it requires preserved failure metadata, bounded retention, alerting, and an idempotent replay mechanism.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Dead Letter Queues before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Configuring an SQS Redrive Policy with `maxReceiveCount = 3` and exponential visibility-timeout backoff moves the malformed webhook to `billing-webhooks-dlq` within 90 seconds, keeping main queue p99 lag under 500ms while alerting on-call.
